intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “Mary Slessor (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It is the true story of a poor Scottish factory girl who sailed to Calabar, in what is now Nigeria, lived among the Okoyong people, rescued twin babies and their mothers, and came to be called “Everybody’s Mother.” It works for a family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and is best for ages 8–12; younger children can join in if a grown-up sits close by.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand so nothing in it takes you by surprise, and have paper, pencils and crayons ready. The book is honest that Mary’s father drank too much, that twin babies were killed because of an old fear, and that many people Mary loved died, so read those parts calmly, answer questions simply and truthfully without adding detail, never ask anyone to talk about troubles at home in front of the group, and keep coming back to the book’s own point: God looked after Mary, made her brave, and used her to save many lives. Speak of the people of Calabar and Okoyong with the same respect the book does; they are Mary’s friends, helpers and church, not a backdrop.

weeks.summary: Mary is born in Aberdeen in 1848 to a gentle, praying mother who reads the Calabar mission news aloud, and little Mary’s pretend school pupils are always Africans. Her father drinks away the family’s money, and though Mary prays for him for years, he never changes; meanwhile the “wild lassie” comes to faith after an old widow speaks to some girls by her fire. Keep the father’s drinking brief and matter-of-fact, as the book does; some children may know this pain at home, so let the chapter’s own line stand (tell a grown-up you trust if you feel unsafe) and offer to talk privately afterwards. The big idea: God is a kind Father in heaven who never lets us down, and we can tell him everything.

memory_verse.text: Like a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him.

activity.title: A Folded Prayer
steps: Give each child a sheet of paper and have them fold it in half like a card.
On the front, have them draw Mary as a “wild lassie,” running and playing in Scotland.
Explain that the inside is just between them and God: no one will look at it or ask about it.
Inside, let them draw or write anything they would like to tell their Father in heaven, then fold it shut to take home.
Say the memory verse together, holding the closed cards.

weeks.summary: At eleven Mary starts work at the Baxter Brothers factory, soon working twelve-hour days, becoming a skilled weaver, and reading a book propped on her loom; when her father dies in 1870, her wages keep the family going. She loves the Bible, gives her own copy away, and teaches rough boys in a poor part of Dundee, where a gang leader swings a lead weight round her head until it brushes her forehead, and she does not move. The big idea: being brave does not mean never feeling scared; Mary was afraid of crowds and even cows all her life, but God helped her stay put and do what was right.

memory_verse.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

activity.title: Stay Put, Mary!
steps: Have the children walk slowly around the room.
Call out something that might make someone nervous, like “A big crowd!”, “A cow in the field!” or “Read aloud to the class!”
When they hear it, everyone freezes, stands tall and says, “God helps me be brave!”
After a few rounds, sit down and remind them that Mary felt scared too, but she stayed put. Say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Mary’s brother John, whom their mother hoped would be a missionary, dies in New Zealand, and a quiet thought grows in Mary: could she go to Africa in his place? Stirred by the news of David Livingstone’s death, she offers herself in 1875, a factory girl who had hardly been to school, and sails in 1876, grieved to see casks of strong drink loaded beside “only one missionary.” The big idea: we do not need to feel brave or clever to say “Here I am” to God; we only need to know that he loves us.

memory_verse.text: I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, here am I; send me.

activity.title: Here I Am Footprints
steps: Have each child stand on a sheet of paper while a partner draws around their shoe.
Inside the footprint, have them write “Here I am. Send me!”
Around the footprint, have them draw one small place God might send them this week: home, school, a friend’s house or a neighbour’s door.
Line the footprints up across the floor like a path and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Mary arrives in Calabar in 1876, learns the Efik language by ear until visitors say she speaks it better than many Efik people, and once rings the bell for morning prayers at moonlight by mistake. At Old Town she meets the old fear of twins: the babies were killed and their mother driven away, though the Efik rulers had already agreed to ban it. Of one pair she rescued, the boy was taken and killed, but the girl, Atim Eso, lived and went to Scotland with Mary, where she was baptised Janie. Tell the twin custom in the book’s own simple words, with no detail, and say plainly that it came from a fear and that many people there wanted it to end. The big idea: God never forgets any child, not even one everyone else turns away.

memory_verse.text: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

activity.title: God Never Forgets Your Name
steps: Sit together in a circle.
Start by turning to the child on your left and saying, “God never forgets [name].”
Have that child turn to their left and say the same, until every name has been said.
Go round again in a whisper, then say the memory verse together.
Ask who might feel left out at school or church, and how the group could make them feel remembered.

weeks.summary: Back in Scotland, Mary cares for baby Janie and her family, moving her sick sister and mother to Topsham, and her mother gives her back to God, saying, “When He needs you and where He sends you, there I would have you be.” Soon after Mary returns to Calabar in 1885, her mother dies, and then her sister Janie; Mary leads the prayer meeting that night and tells no one. Her house fills with rescued children again, including a baby whose mother had died. Some children will be missing someone, so keep the talk gentle and never press for names. The big idea: when we are very sad God does not tell us to stop crying; he stays close and is our strength when we have none left.

memory_verse.text: My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

activity.title: A Strength-of-My-Heart Card
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper to make a card.
On the front, have them draw a big heart and colour it in brightly.
Inside, help them write “God is the strength of your heart,” and sign their name.
Suggest they give it to someone who might be sad or missing someone, or keep it for themselves.
Pray together for everyone who misses someone they love.

weeks.summary: Mary is sent to Okoyong, a forest country no missionary lived in, where an important man’s death could mean others were killed to go with him; mention this only in passing. On 4 August 1888 she lands near dark with five crying children, and in the black forest she is too scared to pray anything but one word, “Father!”, which is enough; she sings silly songs to cheer the children, walks back barefoot for the luggage, and stays. The big idea: when we are too scared to say much, one word like “Father!” is a real prayer, and God hears it.

memory_verse.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and of good courage; don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.

activity.title: The One-Word Prayer
steps: If you can, dim the lights a little and have everyone sit quietly.
Name times when someone might feel scared: a thunderstorm at night, a bad dream, a first day at a new school, getting lost in a shop.
After each one, have the children point up and whisper, “Father!”
Turn the lights up and teach the memory verse with actions: strong arms for “be strong,” shake heads for “don’t be afraid,” and arms wide for “wherever you go.”

weeks.summary: In Ekenge Mary shares one small room with five children, with cows behind the wall, and is never left alone, so she prays out loud by chopping bushes with a machete. Chief Edem’s sister, Ma Eme, gruff in the yard but gentle with Mary, becomes her secret helper, risking her own life to warn Mary when someone was about to be hurt, using a medicine bottle as their signal; their friendship lasts twenty-five years, though Ma Eme never became a Christian. The big idea: God often sends friends we would never expect, and he wants us to be brave, kind friends too. Ma Eme is the brave heroine of this chapter, so let the children admire her.

memory_verse.text: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

activity.title: Our Secret Kindness Signal
steps: Put the children in pairs and have each pair make up a secret friendly signal, like a double thumbs-up or a tap on the shoulder, that means “I’ll help you.”
Read out everyday moments, such as “Someone drops all their books,” “Someone is sitting alone at lunch,” or “Someone can’t find their coat.”
After each one, have the pairs give their signal and say together one way they would help.
Finish by thanking God for friends, and for Ma Eme’s courage.

weeks.summary: When Chief Edem’s son Etim dies after an accident with a log, people blame witchcraft and bring over a dozen prisoners from another village to be made to drink poison. Mary dresses Etim for his funeral in silk to honour the family, sits with the prisoners day and night with the carpenter Charles Ovens, prays until her fear goes, refuses to move from the yard, and at last whispers “Ifehe!” (“Run!”) to a woman and runs with her to safety; Ma Eme pleads for another, the prisoners are freed, and no one is killed at the funeral. Read the poison part plainly and briefly, and do not act any of it out; note Chief Edem’s words, “We are all weary of the old customs.” The big idea: sometimes being brave means staying put and saying no, and God can give us courage to stand up for someone in danger.

memory_verse.text: Rescue the weak and needy. Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.

activity.title: A Courage Shield
steps: Have each child draw a big shield shape filling a sheet of paper.
Across the top, help them write “God gives me courage.”
In the middle, have them draw one way to stand up for someone, like sitting with a child who is left out, saying “Stop, that’s unkind,” or telling a teacher.
Hold the shields up together and say the memory verse.

weeks.summary: Mary’s house becomes a safe place for babies, and when many die she buries each with flowers and a prayer, crying for every one. When a slave woman named Iye has twins and is driven out, Mary runs barefoot to meet her, carries the babies herself, and has a new path cut so Iye need not walk through the village; the boy had already died, but the girl, Susie, lives and becomes the darling of the house until an accident with boiling water, when Mary nurses her for thirteen days before she dies in Mary’s arms. Then the village gathers at a twin’s grave to praise God, and Mary pays to set Iye free. This is a sad chapter, so read slowly, allow quiet, and do not linger on Iye’s treatment or Susie’s injury. The big idea: Jesus is a shepherd who carries his lambs close to his heart, and no one is too small for his love.

memory_verse.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, [and] will gently lead those who have their young.

activity.title: Gathering the Lambs
steps: Have the children spread out around the room and sit down as little lambs.
Walk among them as the shepherd, and gently call each lamb by name to come and join you in a circle, the “fold.”
When everyone is gathered, say together, “No one is too small for Jesus to carry.”
Close by praying quietly for babies and children who are sick or alone.

weeks.summary: Mary walks eight hours through pouring rain to help a dying chief, losing her boots, stockings and umbrella, so that no one in his household will be killed; the chief recovers, and that silly, soaking walk wins the Okoyong people’s hearts more than anything else. When a war is about to start she goes anyway, answering a chief’s scorn with, “you have evidently forgotten to take into account the woman’s God,” and the very chief she had helped kneels and asks her to make peace. Afterwards people bring her their quarrels, and she sits in the middle of the shouting quietly knitting. The big idea: Jesus calls peacemakers God’s children, and we can help people stop fighting and be friends again.

memory_verse.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

activity.title: What Would a Peacemaker Do?
steps: Show the children how to pretend to knit, slowly and calmly, the way Mary did while people argued.
Read out small everyday quarrels, such as “Two friends both want the red crayon” or “Someone pushed in the queue.”
While everyone keeps knitting, ask the group how a peacemaker could help, and listen to a few answers.
Finish by saying the memory verse together, quietly, like Mary’s clicking needles.

weeks.summary: The people move to Akpap in 1896; a sickness kills four of Mary’s children, smallpox spreads, and Mary vaccinates people and turns her old house into a hospital while almost everyone else runs away. When Chief Edem dies of smallpox, she makes his coffin, digs his grave and buries her old friend herself, then works alone for three dark years, writing, “All is dark, except above. Calvary stands safe and sure.” In August 1903, fifteen years after she came, seven young people and eleven children are baptised, and everyone sings Psalm 103 in Efik. Keep the deaths brief and give the most time to the joyful baptism. The big idea: God is at work even in the dark, and joy comes in the morning.

memory_verse.text: For his anger is but for a moment; his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.

activity.title: Night and Morning
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper in half.
On the left half, have them colour a dark night sky with a moon and stars.
On the right half, have them draw a bright sunrise, and children singing.
Help them write across the bottom, “Joy comes in the morning,” and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Mary sends Esien, Effiom and Mana, a girl once sold as a slave, to teach at Itu, where hundreds soon come to the church they built; she lays cement floors herself, praying as she stirs, and in her sixties is pushed through the bush in a basket-chair, saying the strength comes each day as she begins. She dies on 13 January 1915 with the girls she raised beside her, mourned as “Everybody’s Mother,” and at her grave her Jamaican friend Mammy Fuller says one word: “Safe.” Mention her death simply and peacefully, as the book does; this is a good week to look back over the whole story. The big idea: Mary was never strong, but God gave her strength for each day, and he will do the same for us. The chapter’s own verse, 2 Corinthians 12:9, is a good one to read aloud too.

memory_verse.text: He gives power to the faint; and to him who has no might he increases strength.

activity.title: Walk Mary’s Journey
activity.materials: Six sheets of paper and a crayon, prepared by the leader
steps: Before the session, write one place on each sheet, “Aberdeen,” “Dundee,” “Calabar,” “Ekenge,” “Akpap” and “Itu,” and spread them around the room in that order.
Walk to each sheet together as a group.
At each one, ask a child to tell one thing that happened to Mary there.
Before moving on, have everyone say together, “God gave her strength.”
At the last sheet, say the memory verse together and thank God for Mary’s life.
